title: Martyr, Musculus, Zanchi define faith without making remitted-sins persuasion the primary act
source_text: CXXII. Promptum est quoque colligere ex fidei definitione, quam tradunt Petrus Martyr, & Volfgangus Musculus, illos non existimasse firmam persuasionem de impetrata a Deo remissione peccatorum, esse primarium & specificum actum fidei salvificae, & illum ipsum quo justificamur: quandoquidem nullam omnino mentionem ejus faciunt in definitione fidei justificantis, quam, ut saepius jam indicavimus, Musculus dicit esse Constantem assensum cordis ad ea quae vel narrantur, vel promittuntur Verbo. Martyr autem, Firmum certumque assensum Verbis Dei, a Spiritu divino afflatum ad salutem credentium. Et per firmum assensum declarat se intelligere, eum qui sit tantarum virium & efficaciae, ut secum trahat affectum fiduciae, spei, charitatis, & omnia tandem bona opera. Ubi per fiduciam intelligit, ut patet, affectum voluntatis, non mentis persuasionem, & illam facit effectum fidei, non vero actum proprium & formalem. Sicut & Musculus exponit credere in Deum, quod ipsi est tertia & potissima fidei pars, per spem omnem in Deum dirigere, firmaque fiducia ab illius bonitate pendere. Ac praeterea certum est ex definitione fidei justificantis, quam ex Zanchio retulimus, illum non constituere proprium & formalem actum fidei justificantis in fiducia seu persuasione de justitia & peccatorum venia quam a Deo consecuti sumus; sed in fiducia de illa obtinenda. Siquidem fidem dicit esse firmum & indubitatum assensum in promissiones Dei, de remissione peccatorum & justitia accipienda, aeternaque vita consequenda a Deo per & propter Christum.
pass_a_gloss: It is also easy to gather from the definition of faith that Peter Martyr and Wolfgang Musculus hand down that they did not think firm persuasion of remission of sins obtained from God to be the primary and specific act of saving faith, and that very act by which we are justified: since they make no mention at all of it in defining justifying faith — which, as we have often noted, Musculus says is a Constant assent of the heart to those things that are either narrated or promised by the Word. Martyr, however: a Firm and certain assent to God's Words, breathed by the divine Spirit unto the salvation of believers. And by firm assent he declares he means one of such strength and efficacy that it draws with it the affection of trust, hope, charity, and finally all good works. Where by trust he plainly means an affection of the will, not a persuasion of the mind, and makes it an effect of faith, not its proper and formal act. So also Musculus explains believing in God — which for him is the third and chief part of faith — as directing all hope to God and depending with firm trust on his goodness. And furthermore it is certain from the definition of justifying faith we reported from Zanchi that he does not place the proper and formal act of justifying faith in trust or persuasion concerning the righteousness and pardon of sins we have obtained from God, but in trust concerning obtaining it. Since he says faith is a firm and undoubted assent to God's promises concerning remission of sins and righteousness to be received, and eternal life to be obtained from God through and for Christ.
pass_b_english: Martyr and Musculus never make already-obtained remission the primary justifying act — their definitions omit it.

Musculus: constant heart-assent to what the Word narrates or promises. Martyr: firm Spirit-breathed assent that draws trust, hope, charity, and good works — trust as will's affection (effect), not mind's persuasion (formal act).
Zanchi locates the formal act in trust of obtaining pardon/righteousness/life through Christ — not persuasion that they are already ours.

lemmas.gloss: an affection of the will, not a persuasion of the mind

choices.english: they make no mention of it at all
choices.why: Silence in classic definitions undercuts opponent's consensus claim.
